question: At a car-engine test rig, a piston's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = t^2 + t, where t is the time in seconds after ignition. Engineers need the speed gained between t = 1 second and t = 3 seconds. That speed applies to a piston with a mass of 38,000 grams. Find the energy this piston carries at that speed, in joules, then subtract 1 from that number. Convert what remains into kilojoules, multiply the result by 7, and then by 7 again. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a car-engine test rig crew reports, in kilonewtons, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 4, and then by 12 more. Before those multiplications, the value was a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that a 121 kilogram connecting rod exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to its speed at t = 2 seconds, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 4t^3 for t in seconds after ignition. (The engine's oil reservoir holds 5 liters, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a model-rocket sled test track, a sled's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 4t^2 + 5t, where t is the time in seconds after launch. Engineers need the speed gained between t = 1 second and t = 2 seconds, and they add 1 to that speed. That total applies to a sled with a mass of 25 kilograms. (The sled's guide rail is 6 meters long, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this sled carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 7, and then by 11. What is the final number, in joules?

The final number a wind-tunnel model lab logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by converting an energy value that had already been multiplied by 3. That unmultiplied energy, in joules, is what a 13,000 gram scale model carries while moving at a speed obtained by multiplying an earlier reading by 3. That earlier reading is itself 16 more than the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both a 186 centimeter cable and a 302 centimeter cable with nothing left over. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

A calibration sheet at a catapult test rig lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a projectile: the two numbers add up to 13 and multiply together to give 42. The correct reading is the larger of the two. That speed applies to a projectile with a mass of 23,000 grams. (The catapult arm is 3.5 meters long, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this projectile carries at that speed, in joules, then add 19 to that number. Convert what results into kilojoules, add 19 more, and then multiply the result by 11. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

At a pinball launcher test rig, the rate at which the plunger's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = 5t^2 + 2t, where t is the time in seconds after release. Engineers need the total acceleration gained between t = 0 and t = 1 second. That acceleration acts on a plunger head with a mass of 82,000 grams. Find the push this plunger head requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Add 28 to the result, and then add 5 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a crane hoist facility crew reports, in kilonewtons, is 14 more than an earlier figure obtained by multiplying a converted force reading by 7. That force, first in newtons, is what a 131 kilogram counterweight exerts while accelerating at a rate that was itself multiplied by 6. The unmultiplied acceleration, in meters per second squared, comes from a test repeated 2 times, where each repetition combines a baseline reading worth 6 units with an extra reading worth 13 units, and adding together the results from both repetitions. (The hoist's motor draws 15 amps, a detail that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a wind turbine nacelle test crew logs, in joules, is 14 more than an earlier figure obtained by multiplying an energy reading by 4, after that reading had already been increased by 27 and by 8. The unadjusted energy, in joules, is what a 27 kilogram calibration mass carries while moving at a speed equal to the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both a 152 centimeter cable and a 373 centimeter cable with nothing left over. What is the final number, in joules?

The final number a robotics-lab technician logs, in joules, is 30 more than an earlier figure obtained by multiplying an energy reading by 11, after that reading had already been multiplied by 2. The unmultiplied energy, in joules, is what a 60,000 gram test arm carries while moving at a speed equal to the number of different groups of 4 servo motors a technician could choose from 8 identical units on the shelf. What is the final number, in joules?

At a pinball launcher test rig, the rate at which the plunger's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = 4t^2 + 6t, where t is the time in seconds after release. Engineers need the total acceleration gained between t = 0 and t = 3 seconds. That acceleration acts on a plunger head with a mass of 50 kilograms. (The plunger spring is rated at 200 newtons per meter, a detail that plays no role here.) Find the push this plunger head requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Add 14 to the result, then multiply what remains by 7, and then by 9. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a model-rocket sled test track crew logs, in joules, is obtained by multiplying an energy reading by 2, after that reading had already been reduced by 20 and by 2. The unadjusted energy, in joules, is what a 24,000 gram sled carries while moving at a speed gained between t = 2 seconds and t = 3 seconds, given that the sled's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 5t^2 + 2t over that interval. What is the final number, in joules?

The final number a flywheel test rig crew reports, in joules, is 20 more than an earlier figure obtained by multiplying an energy reading by 2, after that reading had already been multiplied by 2. The unmultiplied energy, in joules, is what a 36 kilogram flywheel segment carries while moving at a speed equal to the larger of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 12 and multiply together to give 35. (The flywheel spins inside a housing rated for 500 volts, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in joules?

A calibration sheet at a satellite-thruster test bay lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a small test mass: the two numbers add up to 3 and multiply together to give 2. The correct reading is confirmed to be the larger of the two. That speed applies to a test mass weighing 18,000 grams. Find the energy this mass carries at that speed, in joules, then convert that number into kilojoules. Multiply the result by 2, and then subtract 23. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a flywheel test rig crew logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 2, after that figure was reduced by 12. Before that reduction, the value was a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value, in joules, carried by a 30 kilogram flywheel segment moving at a speed obtained by multiplying an earlier reading by 11. That earlier reading, in meters per second, is the larger of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 9 and multiply together to give 8. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a robotic-arm joint test bench crew records, in kilonewtons, is obtained by multiplying a converted force figure by 10. That figure, in kilonewtons, came from converting a force value in newtons that had already been multiplied by 7. The unmultiplied force is what a 116,000 gram housing exerts while accelerating at a rate obtained by multiplying an earlier reading by 2. That earlier reading, in meters per second squared, is how sharply the joint's motion is changing at t = 1 second, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 3t^3 + 6t^2 for t in seconds after actuation. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a model-rocket sled test track, a sled's position, in meters, follows s(t) = 2t^3 - t^2, where t is the time in seconds after launch. Engineers need the sled's speed at t = 1 second. That speed applies to a sled with a mass of 29 kilograms. (The sled's parachute pack is stored in a 0.3 cubic meter compartment, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this sled carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 5, then add 17, then multiply what remains by 2, and then by 10. What is the final number, in joules?

The final number a car-engine test rig crew logs, in kilojoules, comes from converting an energy value that is 21 more than an earlier figure, itself obtained by multiplying an energy reading by 7 and then by 2. The unmultiplied energy, in joules, is what a 50,000 gram piston assembly carries while moving at a speed obtained from a bench test repeated 8 times, where each repetition combines a baseline reading worth 4 units with an extra reading worth 2 units, and adding together the results from all 8 repetitions. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a wind-tunnel model test lab logs, in kilojoules, is 18 more than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value that had been reduced by 9 and then by 11. The unadjusted energy, in joules, is what a 57,000 gram scale model carries while moving at a speed gained between t = 0 and t = 3 seconds, given that the model's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 3t^2 over that interval. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a model-rocket sled test track crew logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a converted energy figure by 4. That figure, in kilojoules, came from converting an energy value that had been reduced by 21 and then by 1. The unadjusted energy, in joules, is what a 9 kilogram sled carries while moving at a speed equal to its speed at t = 3 seconds, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 2t^3 + 4t^2 for t in seconds after launch. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a satellite-thruster test bay crew reports, in kilonewtons, comes from converting a force value that had been multiplied by 4. The unmultiplied force is 10 less than an earlier reading, which is the push a 194,000 gram thruster housing exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the larger of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 10 and multiply together to give 24. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a robotic-arm joint test bench crew reports, in kilonewtons, is 8 more than a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that a 116,000 gram housing exerts while accelerating at a rate that is 29 more than a total. That total is found by adding up the square of k for k = 1 through 4 -- that is, 1 squared plus 2 squared plus 3 squared plus 4 squared. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

A calibration sheet at a conveyor-belt test bench lists two candidate acceleration readings, in meters per second squared, for a gearbox housing: the two numbers add up to 8 and multiply together to give 15. The correct reading is the larger of the two, and subtracting 3 from it gives the actual acceleration of a housing with a mass of 106,000 grams. (The conveyor belt itself runs at 240 volts, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then subtract 6 from that number. Convert what remains into kilonewtons, and then add 23 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a flywheel test rig crew reports, in kilonewtons, is 24 more than a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that had been multiplied by 10. The unmultiplied force is what a 183,000 gram flywheel segment exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the larger of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 12 and multiply together to give 35. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a wind turbine nacelle test rig, two support cables measure 263 centimeters and 249 centimeters. Technicians want the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both cables with nothing left over, and that length becomes the speed, in meters per second, of a calibration mass with a mass of 34,000 grams. (The nacelle housing is rated to withstand winds of 45 meters per second, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this mass carries at that speed, in joules, then add 4 to that number, then add 29 more, then add 8 more, and then convert the result into kilojoules. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a robotic-arm joint test bench crew logs, in kilonewtons, comes from converting a force value that is 6 more than an earlier figure, which is itself 26 more than a force reading a 43 kilogram housing exerts while accelerating at a rate obtained by multiplying an earlier reading by 11. That earlier reading, in meters per second squared, is the joint's speed at t = 1 second, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 3t^3 - t^2 for t in seconds after actuation. (The joint's mounting bracket is 0.4 meters long, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
